paragraphs.heading: How oxygen gets in and out
paragraphs.text: Oxygen enters the ocean at the surface. It comes from photosynthesis by phytoplankton and from mixing with the atmosphere. Living things, from microbes to many-celled organisms, use oxygen in respiration through the whole depth of the ocean. When the supply from the surface is smaller than the amount used in deep water, oxygen is lost. This is natural, but more layering and warmer water make it worse.

paragraphs.heading: Layers that do not mix
paragraphs.text: Stratification is the layering of water masses that differ, mainly in temperature and salinity, with less dense water lying on top of denser water. The bigger the differences between layers, the less they mix. Stratification grows when the surface ocean warms or when more fresh water arrives from rivers and melting ice. That cuts the supply of oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: Warm water holds less
paragraphs.text: Solubility also limits supply. As temperature and salinity go up, the solubility of oxygen goes down, meaning less oxygen can dissolve in water as it warms and gets saltier. Warmer water is also more buoyant than cooler water. This leads to less mixing between oxygen-rich water near the surface and deeper water, which naturally has less oxygen. Warmer water raises the oxygen demand of living organisms too, leaving less available for marine life.

paragraphs.heading: Oxygen minimum zones
paragraphs.text: The open ocean has natural low-oxygen areas called oxygen minimum zones. They generally lie in the middle depths, from 100 to 1000 m down. They form naturally, through the respiration of sinking organic material that was produced in the surface ocean. Water circulates slowly in these areas. As the ocean's oxygen content falls, the zones are expanding both vertically and horizontally.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of oxygen loss
paragraphs.text: Ocean deoxygenation is the drop in oxygen content in parts of the ocean caused by human activities. It comes in two types, in different zones and with different causes. In coastal zones, a process called eutrophication has driven oxygen down to very low levels quite quickly, within a few decades; these areas are also called dead zones. In the open ocean, oxygen levels are falling, and as a result the natural low-oxygen zones are slowly growing, an expansion that follows from human-caused climate change.

paragraphs.heading: How much, and who is affected
paragraphs.text: Studies show that 1-2% of the oxygen in the oceans has already gone since the middle of the 20th century. Model simulations predict a decline of up to 7% over the next hundred years, and the decline is projected to go on for a thousand years or more. Less oxygen is a threat to marine life and to people who rely on it for food or a living. It changes the ocean's productivity, the way nutrients and carbon move around, and the way marine habitats work.
